newsitem.title: USA: Dow Corning plans $3 billion breast implant settlement.
newsitem.headline: Dow Corning plans $3 billion breast implant settlement.

text.p: Dow Corning said Monday it has filed a bankruptcy reorganization plan under which it would pay up to $2 billion to consumers and $1 billion to companies to settle claims of damages from silicone breast implants.
The company said it would set aside $600 million to settle lawsuits by thousands of women that drove the company to file Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in May 1995.
Another $1.4 billion would be available if women who received implants can prove in a scientific trial that the implants caused disease, the company said.
Dow Chemical and Dow Corning Corp., a joint venture with Corning Inc., have been sued by thousands of women who allege the implants have caused medical problems such as connective tissue diseases.

In the reorganization plan, filed with the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Bay City, Mich., Dow Corning said its plan provides choices for women with implants on how to resolve their claims with flexible options while preserving their right to a jury trial if they want it.

The Midland, Mich.-based company said it believes that the scientific evidence does not support the claim that breast implants cause disease. However, it said it recognises that this is a controversial issue and has proposed a "causation trial" as an objective, streamlined mechanism to resolve it.

As a result, Dow Corning proposed that a court-appointed, independent panel of doctors and scientific experts assess all available studies to determine if there is legitimate and sufficient proof of a connection between silicone breast implants and disease.
A jury should hear testimony from the scientific panel to decide whether claims that breast implants cause disease should be compensated by Dow Corning, it said.

"The plan also provides fair treatment for all women by eliminating any bias in favour of who was first with a court date, who filed in a specific court, or with a specific attorney," said Richard A. Hazleton, chairman and chief executive of Dow Corning.

"The plan demonstrates our commitment to treat everyone with legitimate claims fairly and at the same time preserves the viability of the company, for our customers, employees and others who rely on us."
The plan offers five settlement choices available over several years to process and resolve the claims.

Women who prove a physical injury arising from a Dow Corning implant could obtain an expedited cash payment. Those who want to have their implants removed could obtain an explant certificate for an explant procedure.

Women with claims that meet an established range of criteria could obtain a cash payment. The precise definition of the criteria and the payment schedule would depend on the outcome of the causation trial, Dow Corning said.
Women could also choose an individual evaluation of their claim, which would require a higher level of proof, including the possibility of an independent medical examination.
Women could also agree on non-binding mediation as an alternative to proceeding with the expense and uncertainty of a jury trial, it said.
Dow Chemical's stock fell 25 cents to $83.50 and Corning rose 50 cents to $41 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday.
